To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

two or more stumblings, one or more falls, spending 4 or more consecutive days in bed, and self‐reported health status were independent predictors of falls in a prospective study of community‐dwelling elders.
two or more stumbls, one or more falls, having spent 4+ days in bed, and self‐reported poor health status were independent risk factors for falls at 12 months.

two or more stumblings in the past month, a history of falls, a recent period of bed rest, and a self‐reported decline in health status were independent predictors of falls among community‐ dwelling elderly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiology of falls among community‐dwellers.
the development of an integrated model for the prevention of falls among the elderly.
the identification of risk factors that may be amenable to prevention or intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
two or more stumblings in the past month, having had one or more falls in the past month and spending four or more days in the past month in bed, are independent predictors of falls.
multiple stumbles, falls, bed confinement, and self‐reported poor health status are independent risk factors for subsequent falls among community‐dwellers.
two or more stumblings, one or more falls, and spending 4 or more consecutive days in bed in a month are independent risk factors for future falls in community‐dwelling, noninstitutionalized elderly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

multiple stumbles are a risk factor for falls among community dwelling elderly and that this risk factor is independent of other factors that have been identified in the literature as risk factors for falls.
the number of falls in the previous year was the best predictor of falls during the next year.

two or more stumblings without a fall in one month, one or more falls in the previous year, spending 4 or more consecutive days in bed, and a decline in health are risk factors for a fall in the following 12 months.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stumbles are a risk factor for future falls.
stumbles, falls, and hospitalization are all important risk factors for future falls in community‐dwelling older adults.
multiple stumbles are an important risk factor for falls in community‐dwelling older people and may be a useful screening tool for identifying those at high risk of falling.
